11276-civil-government-in-the-united-sta:
John Fiske's 1890 textbook, Civil Government in the United States, explains American institutions by their origins, not only their present shape. Fiske, asked by Houghton, Mifflin to write a small book useful in schools and suggestive to general readers. adopts a historical method: he shows how institutions acquired their form and keep adapting to new conditions. Epigraphs from Pindar and Longfellow's Ship of State frame the work.

The book dedicates itself to hundreds of young friends Fiske met in studies of American history. Its argument is that government is perpetually modified, never finished. Generations of students learned civics from Fiske's clear, patriotic prose, and the book remains a readable introduction to federal, state, and local government.
15110-lessons-of-the-war-being-comments-:
Spenser Wilkinson's 1900 book gathers weekly comments on the Boer War, written from its eve on October 11, 1899, through the relief of Ladysmith. He frames the war as a fight for supremacy in South Africa between the Boer states and the British Empire, and he warns that weak policy leads to bad strategy. Buller's problems get close attention.

Later chapters follow delay, defeat, and collapse of Boer power, with pleas for the right commander and a clear national purpose. Wilkinson writes as a strategist for newspaper readers, not a memoirist. The book stands as a sharp, contemporary record of how Britain argued about its war week by week.
18602-the-fourth-r:
George O. Smith wrote this science fiction novel, first published in 1959 and reprinted by Dell in 1979. Its hero, James Quincy Holden, is five years old at the start, yet already talks like a grown scholar. At his birthday party he sips ginger ale while adults drink cocktails, wins at bridge, and debates his father on chance, logic, and the laws of games.

The book follows a child prodigy whose mind outruns his years, with gifts such as Kipling tales, a planetarium, and a geiger counter kit hinting at his bent. Smith writes with humor and a taste for bright talk. The novel is a clever, old-style tale of a super-bright boy.
19913-omaha-dwellings-furniture-and-impl:
Alice Fletcher and Francis La Flesche documented Omaha life for the Bureau of Ethnology. This study of dwellings, furniture, and implements appeared in the Thirteenth Annual Report. The Omaha's primitive homes were chiefly earth lodges. Bark or mat lodges came second in their account. Skin lodges, or tipis, served for travel and hunting. No sacred rites attached to lodge-building among the Omaha and Ponka, they note.

La Flesche, himself Omaha, gave the work insider knowledge. Fletcher's measurements and plans set an ethnographic standard. Houses encode kinship, season, and ceremony in their forms. The report preserves building knowledge elders still held then. It remains a foundation source on Omaha material culture.
20456-notes-on-certain-maya-and-mexican-:
Notes on Certain Maya and Mexican Manuscripts is a scholarly paper from the Third Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology. It studies the picture writings left by the Maya and the peoples of Mexico. Scholars of the time were just learning to read these old books.

The writer had lately obtained Léon de Rosny's work on the written documents of ancient America. It held a photo-lithographic copy of two plates, or rather one plate in two parts. Comparing such copies was the only way to study codices kept in distant libraries. The paper shows early American archaeology at work.
2096-a-smaller-history-of-greece-from-th:
William Smith, the great Victorian compiler of classical reference works, writes a compact history of Greece from its earliest times to the Roman conquest. Geography, the heroic age, and national institutions open the book. Smith wrote smaller histories for schools, cutting his larger works down to classroom size.

Chapters then follow Sparta and Athens, the colonies, and the Persian Wars from the Ionic Revolt to Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea. Smith keeps the narrative clear and schoolroom-ready, and the volume still serves as a sound first history. The Greek chapters move briskly from myth to history, so pupils meet heroes before they meet politics.
21725-the-coxswain-s-bride-also-jack-fro:
Three tales by R. M. Ballantyne sit together in this volume, and the first follows lifeboat coxswain Robert Massey. Sturdy Bob, his mates call him, and handsome Bob to the women of his village. He leads the Greyton lifeboat, and his bride-to-be, a fair-haired fisher girl, waits ashore. Their smooth courtship opens the story on a calm, bright evening.

Storm and wreck soon test the coxswain and his crew, as lifeboat tales must. The two shorter tales that follow, Jack Frost and Sons and A Double Rescue, keep to Ballantyne's home ground of sea, weather, and brave deeds. Together they show his range in short form: love, duty, and rescue on a hard coast.
22457-the-verbalist-a-manual-devoted-to-:
Alfred Ayres wrote The Verbalist, a manual on speaking and writing with propriety. Its subtitle promises brief discussions of rules for good usage. Ayres corrects errors of grammar, wording, and pronunciation throughout.

His authorities fill a shelf of nineteenth-century language books. Bain's and Quackenbos's composition grammars stand among his sources. Cobbett's and Goold Brown's English grammars also guide him. Graham's and Crabb's books of synonyms settle fine word choices. Bigelow's Handbook of Punctuation handles stops and marks. The Verbalist distills all that learning into short, firm rulings. It preserves an age when correct English felt like a moral duty to many.
24086-over-the-rocky-mountains-wandering:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote this short adventure book for young readers of modest means, one of a set of small volumes sold for a shilling or two. Its hero is Will Osten, called Wandering Will, who comes home from a long trip to find his father dead. A bequest made during the California gold rush gave Will's father land there.

Will gathers friends and sets out to look at the property, so the tale turns to the life of miners in the gold country. A young lady Will met on an earlier voyage also crosses his path, and he must raise his fare home to England in a hurry. The book gives young readers travel, gold-rush scenes, and a hero always on the move.
24594-letter-to-the-reverend-mr-cary-con:
George Bethune English wrote this letter to the Reverend Mr. Channing, printed at Boston for the author in 1813. English had read Channing's two eloquent sermons on infidelity with interest, and he understood that their appearance owed something to a book he himself had lately published.

With deference and respect, English takes up arguments in the sermons where the reasoning seems less unexceptionable than the language. His letter is a polite but pointed piece of early American religious debate. Readers interested in Unitarian history will find it a sharp, courteous example of pamphlet argument.
26319-a-text-book-of-the-history-of-arch:
A. D. F. Hamlin's Text-Book of the History of Architecture, here in a seventh edition revised in 1909, served college students in the series edited by John C. Van Dyke. Hamlin, professor at Columbia, packed the volume with 229 pictures and diagrams, plus bibliographies, a glossary, and an index of architects. A restored Parthenon fronts the book.

Mid-book pages compare Anglo-Norman churches with French Norman work, setting Waltham and Peterborough beside Cerisy-la-Foret. Hamlin notes that English builders meant to vault their naves but mostly kept wooden roofs, with Durham, Norwich, and Gloucester vaulted only later. The book surveys building from antiquity onward, in clear order for classroom use.
29194-g-r-r-r:
Roger Arcot wrote this fantasy story about Brother Ambrose, a monk who has borne a thousand injuries with humility and charity. Insults, however, are more than he can suffer. Each time Brother Lorenzo heads for his beloved geraniums, watering pot in hand and devotions whispered from saintly lips, Ambrose's hatred seethes. The very fact that Lorenzo lives seems a mockery of justice.

Arcot frames the tale with an aged manuscript, De Necromantiae, and a wish, not too repressed, to pledge one's soul to the Devil. Strange memories and frustrated souls fill this fantastic universe. Readers get a darkly comic monk's tale, where petty hatred curdles into a bargain with evil, told with a growl in its title.
29341-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
Francis J. Reynolds edited this fifth volume of The Story of the Great War, a history of the European war from official sources, covering the Battle of Jutland among its subjects. It is the fifth of eight volumes, illustrated with drawings, maps, and photographs. A second-anniversary section prints statements from the British, French, and German ambassadors to the United States.

Parts cover Austrian propaganda, operations on the sea, the campaign on the eastern front, and the Balkans. Later parts treat the Austro-Italian campaign, the Russo-Turkish campaign, Mesopotamia and Persia, the western front, and the war in the air. Readers get a contemporary illustrated history of the war at sea and on land, written from official sources in the war's second year.
30025-rugs-oriental-and-occidental-antiq:
Rosa Belle Holt wrote Rugs, Oriental and Occidental, Antique and Modern, a handbook for ready reference, in a new and enlarged edition printed in Chicago in 1908. The copyright runs from 1901 to 1908, and the enlarged edition appeared on October 10, 1908. Thirty-three full-page pictures, twelve in full color, with other drawings and a map of the Orient, fill the book.

A front picture shows an antique Tabriz silk rug owned by Mrs. L. G. Burnham of Boston. Its panels mark mosque floor squares for kneeling worshippers, with Tree of Life forms and a rich border. Six chapters treat rug weaving in Egypt, Persia, and Turkey, then India, Afghanistan, and Beluchistan, with miscellaneous rugs and weaving in Europe and America. Holt notes that the first edition of 1901 stood almost alone in its field.
33280-civil-war-experiences-under-bayard:
Henry C. Meyer's memoir records his Civil War service under Bayard, Gregg, Kilpatrick, Custer, Raulston, and Newberry during 1862, 1863, and 1864. A captain of the 24th New York Cavalry and brevet-major of New York Volunteers, Meyer privately printed the book in 1911. Its chapters move from enlistment and first picket duty to Cedar Mountain, Brandy Station, and the second battle of Bull Run.

Meyer writes as a cavalry officer who saw the war from the saddle, noting deaths, raids, and acts of courage among his men. The memoir's strength is its close, dated detail, chapter by chapter. For readers of Civil War history, it is a valuable first-hand record of cavalry service in the eastern campaigns, told by a man who lived it.
33314-h-r:
Edwin Lefevre's novel H. R., published in 1915, centers on a man who made a woman famous, a scene captured in its frontispiece of a woman petrified at the sight of him. Lefevre, author of Sampson Rock of Wall Street, writes of New York life, fame, and the price of success, with a sharp eye for business and society. The book is dedicated to Robert Hobart Davis, a friend whose support Lefevre warmly notes.

The tale moves through studios, offices, and drawing rooms, where talent, luck, and will decide who rises. Its hero, known only by his initials in the title, embodies the self-made man of the age. For readers who enjoy novels of American ambition, the novel offers a brisk, knowing portrait of fame and its costs.
33334-the-only-woman-in-the-town-and-oth:
Sarah J. Prichard's Only Woman in the Town and Other Tales of the American Revolution, published in 1898, gathers stories of the war as seen by women and townsfolk. Prichard, author of a history of Waterbury, writes of a town where one woman stands alone, and of other episodes where ordinary people face invasion, loss, and loyalty. The book was issued by a Daughters of the American Revolution chapter.

The tales' charm lies in their local, human scale, where the Revolution is felt in kitchens and streets rather than on battlefields alone. Prichard writes with warmth for her subjects and care for fact. For readers of Revolutionary lore, it is a pleasing collection of short, true-flavored stories from Connecticut and beyond.
33470-the-forge-in-the-forest-being-the-:
Charles G. D. Roberts's Forge in the Forest, copyrighted in 1896, tells the narrative of Jean de Mer, Acadian ranger and Seigneur de Briart, and how he crossed the Black Abbé. Its frontispiece shows Marc seated on a block just inside a door, a quiet scene before adventure. Roberts, writing of a province whose honored sons he praises, sets his tale in a strange fellowship of forest and forge.

The novel blends history with romance, as Jean moves through Acadian lands, facing foes, friends, and the hard choices of a ranger's life. Its prose is rich and evocative, suited to readers who love Canadian historical fiction. For fans of Roberts, The Forge in the Forest offers a vivid, old-fashioned tale of courage in a wild land.
4230-tom-swift-and-his-motor-cycle-or-fu:
Victor Appleton opened the Tom Swift series with this boys' adventure. Young inventor Tom Swift gets his first motor-cycle and is drawn into a mystery. A reckless ride, a smash-up, and a talk overheard in the dark set him on a chase. Suspicious men in an automobile join the pursuit.

The chase runs through storms, a strange mansion, and a final capture. Tom rides to Albany and follows clues with his hired man Eradicate. He faces a vindictive tramp and a gang of thieves. The book is also a period piece, full of early motor-cycles, touring cars, and a young inventor hero.
667-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words beginning with R. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from R, the dog's letter that hurreth in sound, through Ra, a roe, and Rab, a mason's rod, and onward. Notes trace Greek, Latin, and Phoenician roots.

R brings a rough music to the page: roaring beasts, road tools, and Latin roots crowd together. Readers meet rare trades beside common verbs, each with its own history. The slice rewards slow browsing, where one letter's words show how English borrowed, bent, and kept its sounds.
7192-charles-philip-yorke-fourth-earl-of:
Lady Biddulph of Ledbury wrote this memoir of her father from the letters and journals he left in her care by his will. He was Charles Philip Yorke, fourth Earl of Hardwicke and vice-admiral in the Royal Navy. She admits her diffidence as a first-time author, yet argues that his varied life and his part in the affairs of his time deserve a fuller record than silence would give.

The memoir follows a naval officer and peer through many posts, letting his own papers speak where they can. Portraits face the text, and the dedication to his grandchildren marks the book as a family trust as much as a public life. Readers meet a man of action seen through a daughter's loyal, careful eye.
8353-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-53-1-co:
Corinth's church was quarrelsome, and Paul's first surviving letter to it answers its troubles in order. Factions, lawsuits, loose morals, chaotic worship, and doubts about resurrection each get a reply, firm but pastoral. The letter's center holds two famous passages: the hymn to love, which outlasts prophecy and tongues, and the long proof that Christ's resurrection grounds the believers' own.

It also preserves the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper. In Challoner's Douay-Rheims wording, Paul's advice keeps its older Catholic dress. For churches and readers, 1 Corinthians remains the practical guide to unity: gifts differ, but love binds, and no gift excuses disorder or pride.
8354-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-54-2-co:
Paul's second letter to Corinth is his most personal writing, and the Douay-Rheims text gives it in Challoner's older English. Writing to a church that doubted him, Paul defends his apostleship. He speaks of beatings, shipwrecks, and a thorn in the flesh he could not remove, and claims that strength shows itself in weakness. The tone swings between tenderness and sharp rebuke.

A warm appeal to give for poor believers in Jerusalem runs through the middle, and the letter closes with a call to examine themselves and live at peace. Readers find Paul the man here, weary and proud and hopeful at once. It is the New Testament letter that most feels like a private letter, written in the heat of a quarrel.
a-smaller-history-of-greece-from-the-ear:
William Smith compresses Greek history for students, from the geography of the land and the heroic age to the Roman conquest. His contents move in clear order: the rise of Sparta and Athens, the Greek colonies, then the Persian Wars from the Ionic revolt through Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea.

Chapters on Athens under Pericles and the three periods of the Peloponnesian War follow, then the Thirty Tyrants, the death of Socrates, Macedon's rise, and the age after Alexander. Smith, a famous classical editor, writes plainly and keeps dates and causes in view. Generations of school readers learned their Greece from this compact, orderly survey.
capek-r-u-r:
Capek wrote R.U.R. in Czech, and Czech readers meet the play here in its first tongue. Artificial workers pour from Rossum's factory to serve mankind. Made only for labor, they gain grievances, leaders, and at last the will to rebel.

The drama, first staged in 1920, coined the word robot for all the world. Beneath the marvel runs a hard question about work and worth. Capek gives even his rebels a claim on pity. In its own language, the play shows its wit and rhythm best, a landmark of Czech letters and of modern drama.
charles-philip-yorke-fourth-earl-of-hard:
Lady Biddulph's memoir of her father, Charles Philip Yorke, Fourth Earl of Hardwicke, Vice-Admiral, draws on the letters and journals he left to her care. Biddulph, his daughter, writes with diffidence, since this is her first experience of such work, but her reasons seem to her unanswerable.

Her father's active, varied life, and the large part he played in his day's affairs, deserve a fuller account than reference works supply. Biddulph presents in outline a capable, energetic Englishman, loyal and devoted to sovereign and country. Readers of naval and Victorian biography will find the memoir a labour of love, rich in letters and journals.
civil-government-in-the-united-states-co:
Civil Government in the United States Considered with Some Reference to Its Origins, by John Fiske, was written at the request of Houghton, Mifflin & Co. as both a textbook and a book for the general reader. Its preface promises a historical method: institutions are shown in their present shape and in their origins. Government, Fiske stresses, changes by slow steps to meet new conditions.

Chapters open with taxation and the meaning of government itself. The township follows, with the New England town-meeting and its selectmen treated as the simplest old form of rule. Each chapter carries questions on the text, further suggestive questions, and a bibliographical note for students who read on.
doe-osti-17008666-2025-annual-report-lab:
Brookhaven National Laboratory issued its 2025 annual report on its Laboratory Directed Research and Development program in September 2026. Martin Schoonen and Kathleen Barkigia head the author list. The volume gathers short summaries of lab funded projects that ended in fiscal year 2025, as the Energy Department requires each year.

Projects range across climate and energy modeling for cities, new routes to medical and research isotopes, and real time data handling on new AI hardware. Other summaries cover particle physics planning, light source work, and tools for later experiments. Read as a whole, the volume shows where the lab placed its own seed funds and what each small team finished.
doe-osti-17033591-a-case-study-compariso:
Danielle Markowski of Los Alamos National Laboratory compares two ways of watching the upper air during a thunderstorm in this case study, issued May 21, 2026. Storms disturb the ionosphere, the charged layer high above Earth, through sound and gravity waves. The storm studied crossed the southeast United States on June 15 and 16, 2023.

Lightning signals from a global detection network probed the lower D region, about 60 to 90 kilometers up. Coastal radar units along the east coast, received near Clemson University, probed the higher F region at the same time. The two records showed a slight linked variation, but data gaps, with lightning data best by day and radar best by night, limit the claim.
doe-osti-17117091-highly-efficient-elect:
Matthew Ruehl and colleagues at Argonne close out a CRADA with Oklo and Deep Isolation on a key step in recycling used reactor fuel, in final report ANL/CFC-C2026-00072. Oxide reduction turns uranium oxide fuel into metal by electrochemical means, ready for pyroprocessing. The partners aimed to make that step faster, cheaper, and easier to watch.

Sensors placed in the cell tracked the change from oxide to metal in real time, matching direct lab checks of the product within 5 percent. New mixed metal oxide anodes outlasted standard platinum ones at lower cost, proven from bench to pilot scale. A redesigned fuel basket raised efficiency, and the gains were built into a pilot module that handles up to 10 kilograms of heavy metal per batch.
doe-osti-17134350-tribal-energy-capacity:
Official rules for the Tribal Energy Capacity Expansion Prize come from the Energy Department Integrated Energy Systems Office, reissued in September 2026 after a full rewrite. The prize helps Tribal communities build the staff skills and plans needed to take part in energy decisions and projects. Up to 6 million dollars in cash plus expert help is on offer. Applications are due 4 December 2026, Alaska time.

Three phases structure the contest. Phase 1 covers capacity needs, with up to 14 winners getting 40,000 dollars and 40 hours of technical help. Phase 2 covers capacity development: up to 14 teams win 200,000 dollars and 150 hours of help, with bonus prizes for multi Tribe teams. Phase 3 covers putting plans into action, at 125,000 dollars per winner.
doe-osti-2583462-final-technical-report-:
Rebecca Bennett and Jackie Petre close out Solar Prize Round 6 in NREL technical report TP-6A50-92828, covering June 2022 through December 2024. The American-Made Solar Prize attacked solar's soft costs, the permitting, financing, and customer hunting that now outweigh hardware. Three linked contests, Ready!, Set!, and Go!, moved teams from idea to prototype to pilot partners, with 4.1 million dollars in cash and vouchers on the table.

The funnel worked as designed. One hundred sixty-six teams entered Ready!, beating the goal of one hundred fifty, and every winner advanced through each stage, a one hundred percent carry-through the administrators count as the headline success. Winners could take up to 650,000 dollars in cash plus laboratory vouchers, backed by the American-Made Network of more than five hundred support organizations. NREL executed the winners' lab agreements in under two months. Competitor feedback for improving future rounds closes the account.
doe-osti-2584728-q-fibre-quarterly-perfo:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2005653, written by Fan (Frank) Fei in May 2025, gives a quarterly progress update on the Q-Fibre project. The project uses fiber optic cables in wellbores to track strain and check the integrity of wells and seals. Fei is the principal investigator, with Eric Matzel and Christina Morency as key researchers, and the Norwegian Geotechnical Institute leads the wider team.

Covering January through March 2025, the update reports work on numerical predictions of fiber optic data along a well. Baseline simulations produced axial distributions of pressure, temperature, and strain. Those distributions serve as synthetic cable data for cases where the cable sits inside casing, behind casing, or in the formation. The work sits in Work Package 3 of a three-year, one-million-dollar Department of Energy effort.
doe-osti-2584739-commission-lt-5-m-spati:
Sabrina Nagel wrote this July 2025 milestone report for Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. It covers work on an x-ray imager built for High Resolution Turbulence tests. The milestone, MRT9203 for the third quarter of fiscal 2025, set a clear goal: an imaging system with spatial detail finer than 5 micrometers, ready for use on the National Ignition Facility.

Nagel sets out the pass criteria, the design path, and the tests used to check the system. To pass, the imager had to prove its detail level and its scintillator timing, known to within plus or minus 5 nanoseconds. The target and the scintillator also had to line up to within plus or minus 10 micrometers, so detail held across the full field of view. Test shots on the real system close the report.
doe-osti-2588287-2024-snl-ktf-annual-sit:
Amy Miller prepared the 2024 Annual Site Environmental Report for Sandia National Laboratories' Kaua'i Test Facility, SAND2025-11060R. The facility, on the Hawaiian island of Kaua'i, is Sandia's rocket launch and flight test site. Federal rules require a public accounting each year of how operations affected the local environment.

Chapters introduce the facility's purpose and history, then track monitoring and compliance through 2024. Routine work runs under standing environmental reviews. One table lists the categorical exclusions the Department of Energy compliance officer cited that year. Routine maintenance and fencing determinations under the National Environmental Policy Act lead the list. Monitoring data and program summaries fill out the record. The format matches Sandia's other site reports, adapted here to a Pacific island test range rather than a desert laboratory.
doe-osti-2589618-simulation-of-deuterium:
Lindsay Gilkey and Alexander Brown simulate what happens when deuterium gas meets a room fire, in Sandia report SAND2025-11710. Deuterium is heavy hydrogen, handled at fusion and isotope facilities. If a leak feeds a fire, some gas burns to heavy water vapor, and safety teams need to know how much converts and where it travels.

The model builds on chamber experiments run in 2023, with fuel pans, a hood, and a metered deuterium feed. Simulation cases track gas that stays in the room against gas that flows out. In one case the conversion share to heavy water was 0.059, and the time-integrated concentration reached about 401 parts per million by volume-seconds at 240 seconds. Results help size ventilation and set release limits.
doe-osti-2998952-fermilab-italian-studen:
Michele Mormile's final report for the Fermilab Italian Student Program, FERMILAB-TM-2918-STUDENT, covers analysis work for the Compact Muon Solenoid experiment at CERN. That detector is being upgraded for the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, which will send far more particles through it. Its new outer tracker uses silicon sensors that must pick out high-momentum tracks on the spot, through built-in stub logic, despite heavy radiation damage.

Mormile's task was the data analysis of three test beam runs on a 2S minimodule, a small prototype tracker piece. The runs used proton beams at the Fermilab Test Beam Facility. He reviewed timing phase choices, finding an optimal phase near 4 nanoseconds for one run, and charted how the sensor performed across the runs. The results feed choices for future test beams and for the tracker modules that will enter the upgraded detector.
doe-osti-2999142-hydrodynamic-coupling-t:
Richard Abrantes, Shawn Pautz and Stephen Bond of Sandia National Laboratories test a radiation transport method in LDRD report SAND2025-12754R. Radiation moving through hot matter meets opacity, the blocking power of the material, which swings wildly with photon energy in jagged line patterns. Standard shortcuts average that pattern away, using Rosseland or Planck mean values, and lose accuracy at middling thickness where neither thin nor thick rules hold.

The rival method, built on Young measures by Haut and co-workers in 2017, keeps the pattern's statistics instead of flattening them. The team ran radiation slab tests in aluminium, copper and krypton under varied heat and density conditions. Work then moved into the SCEPTRE transport code and the multiphysics ALEGRA code for coupled radiation and material runs. At equal computing cost, the homogenised method beat both mean-opacity rivals throughout. The coupled run was the first of its kind.
doe-osti-2999147-regulatory-consideratio:
Steven Horowitz of Sandia examines how a future American fuel reprocessing plant should be guarded, in report SAND2025-12527R, prepared in September 2025 for a safeguards program. Advanced reactor vendors may reprocess fuel on site. That means holding formula quantities of special nuclear material, the class the rules guard most strictly. Yet the Nuclear Regulatory Commission has never written a framework for commercial reprocessing, so licensing certainty does not exist.

Horowitz reviews past security rulemaking for a technical base, then proposes risk informed protection rules. Two ideas do heavy lifting. Material hot enough to meet a self protecting radiation dose line might face sabotage rules only, not theft rules. Dilute material, spread thin in other matter, could earn a theft goal based on detection and prompt recovery. A product kept below set uranium and plutonium shares may fit that lighter class. Public safety stays the stated test throughout.
doe-osti-3000945-applying-mechanistic-co:
Scott Cushing of Caltech, with co-investigators including Theo Agapie and Ryan Hadt, files the final report for award DE-SC0022089, covering September 2021 to August 2025. The project builds qubits out of molecules. Unlike solid-state devices, molecular qubits can be tuned atom by atom by chemists, and they sense their chemical surroundings, a natural fit for biological and chemical sensing. Working at room temperature is the prize.

A co-design loop of theory, spectroscopy and synthesis probed how a qubit's spin talks to molecular vibrations, to neighbouring spins and to its environment. Phase I produced record room-temperature coherence for microwave qubits, multi-metal qubits with tunable coupling, and the first theoretical route to all-organic optical qubits. Phase II pushed designs further across optical, organic and multi-centre systems. The report lists accomplishments, publications and the design rules that emerged: mechanistic understanding first, then molecules built to order.
doe-osti-3001950-calibration-and-validat:
DOE report DOE/SC-ARM-TR-322, issued in September 2025 for the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) user facility, covers the calibration and validation of the SAIL radar. V. Chandrasekar, F. Junyent, and S. Biswas, all at Colorado State University, wrote it. SAIL is a field campaign radar, and its X-band scanning radar is called XSAIL.

One part calibrates the radar with a target simulator, a device that feeds the radar a known signal. Another part checks reflectivity and differential reflectivity, two measures of how strongly rain returns the radar beam. The checks use drop size data from ground instruments called disdrometers. Monthly bias results run from November 2021 to June 2023. Radar users rely on checks like these before trusting rainfall numbers.
doe-osti-3002016-deploying-adversarial-a:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/4263, by Emma J. Reid, Haley Duba-Sullivan, Kieran Barr, Steven R. Young, and co-authors, tests whether image super-resolution software can be attacked. Super-resolution models sharpen low-quality images for uses like remote sensing and disaster analysis. The October 2025 report asks what happens when an attacker quietly poisons that sharpening step.

The team built attacks into common open-source super-resolution models. Their targeted attacks cut classifier accuracy on one chosen class by 46 to 72 percent, depending on training stage. Other classes stayed nearly untouched, and image quality stayed high. The attacks need no access to the low-resolution image or its labels when used. The authors note the fakes are still visible to the human eye and call for a detector.
doe-osti-3002270-characterization-and-qu:
Kun Wang, with Mikhail A. Sokolov, Tim Lach, and colleagues, reports a visiting faculty project in Oak Ridge letter report ORNL/LTR-2025/3981, dated 2025. The project studied radiation damage in reactor pressure vessel steels. Neutron exposure forms tiny clusters and precipitates inside the steel, and those clusters make the vessel wall brittle over decades of service.

Surveillance steel samples, from both base metal and welds, were annealed at 340, 450, and 500 degrees Celsius for up to 168 hours. A scanning transmission electron microscope with X-ray spectroscopy mapped the clusters. Machine learning then cleaned and quantified the maps, giving cluster makeup and distribution. The work was done under the DOE Visiting Faculty Program with Alfred University. Better cluster counts sharpen the models that predict vessel embrittlement.
doe-osti-3003134-southern-ocean-aerosols:
P. Edwards, E. Grant, S. Young, and S. Rogers, all at the University of York, report a measurement campaign in ARM report DOE/SC-ARM-25-024, dated November 2025. The campaign measured aerosols over the Southern Ocean, among the cleanest air on Earth. Aerosols there strongly affect cloud brightness and climate, yet ships and aircraft sample the region rarely.

The report records what the team deployed and measured for the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement archive. Its reference list leans on work valuing remote marine aerosol data for cutting uncertainty in radiative forcing: how aerosols shift Earth's energy balance. Aircraft sulfur dioxide comparisons between clean and polluted marine air figure in the background. Field campaign reports serve later analysts, who need to know instrument setup and conditions before trusting the numbers.
doe-osti-3011903-acoustic-tomography-sys:
An acoustic tomography array is installed at the National Wind Technology Center in a CRADA final report by Patrick Moriarty of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. The University of Colorado CIRES system measures complex flow fields around wind turbine arrays, which affect farm output and reliability. Nine freestanding towers of 9.1 metre height carry microphones and speakers.

A centre tower holds a sonic anemometer and a temperature probe. The University of Colorado Boulder is the agreement party, and the report date is September 9, 2025. The record notes there is currently no funding to test and research the installed system.
doe-osti-3020311-joint-modeling-of-water:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory white paper PNNL-38622, by Christopher M. Chini and four co-authors, makes the case for modeling water and power systems together instead of separately. Each utility models its own network well, but the tools barely speak to each other. Power models shrink water systems to single nodes, and water studies use simplified prices, so neither side can plan for the other.

The stakes showed during Winter Storm Uri in Texas in 2021, when power failures put up to 14 million residents under boil-water orders. The paper maps opportunities to run water systems as flexible loads, shifting pumping and treatment, including energy-hungry desalination and water reuse, to help the grid. Coupled models would let decision makers prepare for joint failures and recover faster after disasters.
doe-osti-3021940-protein-engineering-for:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory abbreviated final report LLNL-TR-2015389, by Dan Park, dated March 2026, reports feasibility study 25-FS-031 on using engineered proteins to recover critical metals beyond the rare earth elements. Electrification is driving demand for metals that are hard to separate chemically. Park's group works with lanmodulins, natural proteins that grip rare earths with over a million-fold selectivity against common metals, and asked whether that grip extends to other valuable ions.

They adapted their SpyCI-LAMBS assay, which immobilizes metal-binding proteins for mass screening, to new targets. A panel of 70 natural and engineered proteins was tested against rare earths, indium, and six first-row transition metals. A natural rare-earth-binding protein bound indium with selectivity comparable to heavy rare earths, an unexpected opening. Substitutions in the protein then tuned that behavior further, pointing toward biological recovery of indium from waste streams.
doe-osti-3022671-towards-robust-calibrat:
LANL report LA-UR-26-21647, by Kirill Velizhanin, addresses a practical bottleneck in explosives modeling. It covers calibrating the AWSD reactive burn model so hydrodynamic runs predict detonation well. Calibration means adjusting rate constants and other parameters until the model matches experiments. But each full pass is expensive, and naive searches waste most of their budget in unpromising regions.

The new algorithm nests two loops. Inner loops calibrate against a cheap approximate model, LsDE, built around an active set of five AWSD parameters. Outer loops then update that approximation using the true model. They check whether the active set has converged. Figures track the loss falling and the four most active parameters settling over successive outer loops. The payoff is a calibration method robust enough to trust on new explosive formulations.
doe-osti-3023124-navigating-united-state:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-25-89608, dated February 2026, maps the United States standards and rules that govern digital energy systems. Megan Jordan Culler, Remy Vanece Stolworthy, Alex Tylecote, and co-authors wrote it as a risk mapping exercise. Digital energy technology, they argue, is moving faster than the security standards meant to cover it.

The survey sorts the landscape into federal policy and mandatory reliability standards, state regulation and utility commission actions, and voluntary standards. Slow code adoption gets attention: groups such as the fire suppression industry warn that older NFPA editions can leave the public at risk, yet multi-year adoption cycles keep old editions in force. The authors urge faster standards work and early use of best practices.
doe-osti-3024219-the-evolving-role-of-de:
Brittany Speetles of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this study of demand charges, NLR/TP-7A40-90964, dated March 2026. With her were Mark LeBel of the Regulatory Assistance Project, Ron Nelson of Current Energy Group, and lab colleagues Joyce McLaren, Daniel Zimny-Schmitt, and Dana Stright. Demand charges bill customers for their peak power draw, not just total energy, and they are a sore point for fast charging businesses whose peaks are brief and high.

The report gives the cost backdrop: direct current fast charging can run 60,000 to 100,000 dollars per plug in investment cost, against 2,000 to 10,000 dollars for Level 2 chargers. Utilities have answered with tools such as discounts tied to utilization, demand charge holidays, and folding demand charges into monthly subscription fees set by customer load traits. Electric vehicle specific rate designs get their own treatment.
doe-osti-3024970-central-hanford-vernal-:
N J Exe and M L Johnson of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions report calendar year 2025 monitoring of vernal pools in central Hanford, HNF-72998, Revision 0, published March 2026. Vernal pools are shallow seasonal wetlands that fill in wet months and dry out, sheltering plants found in few other settings. Crews surveyed the pools pool by pool and recorded species cover, flagging each plant as native, exotic, or invasive.

The Gable Butte complex, in the butte's central part, holds ten pools, but Pool 4 splits into three sub-pools at low water, so the survey treats twelve. Entries like brome fescue at a quarter percent cover show the record's grain: dozens of species listed with small cover values, the exotic and invasive ones marked. Year over year, those tables are how managers spot a pool slipping toward weeds.
doe-osti-3363537-taming-the-wild-west-as:
Paul A. Ullrich of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory writes this abbreviated report (LLNL-TR-2017472, May 2026) on the crowded market for impacts-relevant climate data. These products take observations and Earth system model output and downscale, debias, validate, and package them for decision makers planning mitigation and adaptation.

So many products have appeared that stakeholders and scientists alike struggle to pick the best one, and with no standard evaluation protocol, choices were often pragmatic rather than sound. Under project 23-ERD-050, the team set out to build foundational capabilities for assessing these products, so that future selection and application rest on evidence rather than convenience.
doe-osti-3365140-aggregation-and-grid-se:
A workshop report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, by Danish Saleem and Charles MaGill, records the Aggregation and Grid Security Workshop, held June 17 and 18, 2025 in Golden, Colorado. About 40 stakeholders attended: virtual power plant operators, aggregators, equipment makers, utilities, testing labs, trade groups, and cybersecurity vendors. Virtual power plants bundle thousands of home batteries, chargers, and solar systems into one grid resource, and nobody clearly owns their cybersecurity.

Sessions mapped how risk is shared among the parties and where practices lag the technology. Top priorities included defining shared cyber responsibilities, using data to understand and reduce risk, and fast-tracking proven technology fixes. Attendees also weighed what a compromised aggregation could do to the bulk power system. The report turns two days of discussion into a work list for the industry.
doe-osti-3374245-united-states-data-cent:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's United States Data Center Energy Usage Report, 2025 Update, dated June 2026, by Sarah J. Smith, Alex Hubbard, Alex Newkirk, Mohan Ganeshalingam, Billie Holecek, Dale Sartor, Michael Mills, and Arman Shehabi, tracks how much power the nation's data centers draw. The update revisits a long-running Berkeley Lab series at a moment when artificial intelligence builds are driving steep growth in server and accelerator shipments.

The team models total energy use and power capacity, then compares its figures with other industry estimates. For future high-end graphics processors, the model counts chips in Nvidia B300-equivalents, since die supply is the binding limit and power use scales with die size. Separate sections work through AI server setups and unit power draws, so readers can see which assumptions move the national total most.
doe-osti-3374755-an-overview-of-arizona-:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory letter report ORNL/LTR-2026/4446, by Hillary Fishler and Varisara Tansakul, gives an overview of Arizona's electric grid resilience. The numbers come from the lab's TASTI-GRID platform. That platform blends outage and utility data to compare counties side by side. The authors stress that the report guides thinking on investment only. It is not a tool for live outage response or repair forecasts.

Context starts with a 2020 grade of C for Arizona infrastructure from the American Society of Civil Engineers. Reported outages were highest in Navajo County, with twenty-two events. La Paz County saw the longest average recovery, at about 321 minutes. Coconino County shows an odd split. It posts the highest share of customers hit, yet one of the shortest recovery times, near fifteen minutes. Rural counties remain the least well measured.
doe-osti-3375391-taming-the-wild-west-as:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory final report LLNL-TR-2017533, by Paul A. Ullrich and dated June 2026, grades the flood of climate data products aimed at planners. The project code is 23-ERD-050. Impacts-relevant data are records that have been downscaled, debiased, and checked for use in local choices. Farms, cities, and grid planners all lean on such products. Yet the products vary wildly in method and quality, a state the title calls a wild west.

The study pits two families of methods against the PRISM reference data set. Statistical downscaling is one family. Dynamical downscaling, which runs a live weather model, is the other. Scores use the Perkins skill score on rain traits such as total rain and storm peak strength. The dynamical methods matched observed features more closely. They also gained more as grid resolution rose.
doe-osti-3375663-wyoming-trails-carbon-h:
The final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-FE0032360, dated June 2026, lays out a roadmap for a carbon hub in Wyoming. Carbon Solutions of Saint Paul ran the project from March 2024 to February 2026. Erin Middleton served as principal investigator. Monica Hernandez-Lara managed the project. A hub would gather carbon dioxide from area plants, then pipe or haul it to deep storage sites. The study tests whether that web pays, and where its lines should run.

The core tool is SimCCSPRO, a system optimizer for capture and storage webs. Feeder models price capture, score rock storage, and route transport. A fresh advance lets the tool mix pipelines, rail, and road in one plan. That mix matters in Wyoming, where sources sit far apart. The roadmap treats the chain as one network, not as lone projects.
doe-osti-3376032-data-center-cybersecuri:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-26-89666, dated February 2026, by Megan Jordan Culler, Alex Tylecote, and Leta Marie Comer, sums up a supplier cohort on data center cyber risk. The cohort sat inside the lab's TADA for States project, a help program on digital assurance. Suppliers of power gear for data centers met as a group. Three themes ran through the talks: cyber defense, supply chain risk care, and new rules on the way.

One top worry was split governance. Duties for a data center's power chain scatter across utilities, builders, landlords, and vendors. Trip settings, alarm response, and change control can fall between those chairs. A utility may watch a site yet lack the right to force a fix. Its one hard tool is full disconnection, a blunt step for a load that can reach gigawatt scale. The summary ends in action plans for the cohort members.
doe-osti-3377122-evaluation-of-rmi-eject:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-25542, issued July 7, 2026, tests a fix for a gap in the FLAG hydrodynamics code. E. A. Hinrichs of the University of New Mexico and the XCP-6 group did the work from December 2025 to January 2026. When a shock crosses a rippled metal surface, it throws off a spray of particles called ejecta. The Richtmyer-Meshkov instability drives that spray. FLAG's ejecta model long could not run on reconstructed interfaces.

That limit shut the model out of many test setups. Hinrichs ran two-dimensional flyer-plate cases to check the path. A flyer slams into a target, and the code tracks the breaking surface. The runs compare ejecta from the rebuilt interface against the older route. Input decks show a tantalum, copper, and tin stack driven at a set flyer speed. The study's aim is wider use of the model, not a new physics claim.
doe-osti-3377790-airports-as-energy-node:
Airports as Energy Nodes, National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5R00-98503 from July 2026, treats a large airport as a power system in its own right. Ten authors are printed, led by Darren Paschedag, Bryan Mentlik, and Kevin Robby, with Rob Hovsapian and Scott Cary among the team. The project name is shortened to ÆNodes.

An airport concentrates runways, terminals, vehicles, and backup power on one site, so it can host generation and storage that serve both the airport and the surrounding grid. The report works through design cases and their costs in detail, comparing options with and without on-site generation. Cost tables in the middle of the document break spending into thousands of dollars by component, down to fractions of a cent per kilowatt-hour for the options studied.
doe-osti-3682464-automated-4d-x-ray-comp:
An automated way to track flaws in printed steel during creep tests is presented in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2026/4787, dated August 2026. Eight authors are printed, led by Amir Ziabari, Rahul Franklin, and Obaid Rahman. Creep tests stretch hot metal slowly until it fails, with pauses for scans. X-ray tomography maps hidden flaws in three dimensions. The hard part is lining up scans so the same flaw can be followed from pause to pause.

Specimens carried built-in markers in their grips: a chamfered corner at one end and an added corner piece at the other. Those lopsided marks break the near symmetry that fools standard alignment methods. Short scans used fewer projections than full scans, then model-based rebuilding sharpened the volumes. One deep-learning model segmented every state the same way. After rupture, both halves still fit in one frame, giving a single flaw history.
doe-osti-3874819-signalgen-a-platform-th: A short technology sheet from Los Alamos, issued September 1, 2026, presents SignalGen by Dharmesh Patel. Signal peptides are short address tags that route proteins to the right cell compartment or out of the cell. SignalGen trains a protein language model on thousands of proteins and their tags. Given a protein, its target spot, and its organism, it predicts the tag most likely to work. The sheet reports about ninety percent accuracy for the all-organism model, at readiness level three.
doe-osti-3943085-imaging-the-products-of:
Sandia National Laboratories staff A. Alec Talin, Thomas Chan, and David Chandler report early work on photographing the products of light-driven chemical reactions. Their report is SAND2026-26532. The goal is to watch water split on a catalyst surface and catch the gases as they leave.

One part uses velocity map imaging, a camera method that tracks how fast charged fragments fly apart. A second part fires laser pulses at niobium-doped strontium titanate to knock molecules off its surface for mass checks. The team did map hydrogen ions from water vapor over the sample, but the signal was weak and faded as runs went on. They state plainly that no firm findings can be drawn yet. The value here is a clear map of what to fix next.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GiesbrechtRicha:
Five writers joined in an investigative article about Richard Giesbrecht, an insurance salesman from Winnipeg. In February 1964, Giesbrecht gave the FBI evidence of a multi-man plot to kill President Kennedy. Later, he said, agent Merle Nelson told him to forget what he had brought them.

A witness with evidence of a plot, told to forget it, is the heart of many assassination controversies. The article examines Giesbrecht's treatment at the Bureau's hands and the evidence he carried. It preserves a Canadian side door into the case, reported by a team of five journalists.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NaimanJasonR_Na: Harold Weisberg, in all likelihood, wrote this letter, dated January 15, 1970, to Jason R. Neiman. Weisberg's letters of that season usually pushed his books, his lawsuits, or his requests for documents. The file keeps the date and the addressee's name only. It does not summarize the letter's business, so no honest account can say which of those subjects this particular letter took up.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PlotkinStevenR_: nsia-PlotkinStevenR Plotkin Steven R: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WroneDavidR_Wro:
David R. Wrone, a historian at the University of Wisconsin, spent years listing nearly everything written about the Kennedy assassination. His annotated bibliography holds 2,376 entries on the killing of John Fitzgerald Kennedy, and each entry carries a note from the author.

A bibliography with notes does more than list titles. Wrone tells the reader what each item is, who wrote it, and why it matters, across books, magazine articles, pamphlets, and official reports. For anyone entering the huge literature on the assassination, his volume works as a map drawn by a scholar who read the territory himself and marked the sound ground.
govdocs-archive_org-spiritual-authority-:
René Guénon published Spiritual Authority and Temporal Power in 1929, a short book with a firm claim. It states the Traditionalist doctrine of the two powers: priesthood above kingship, spiritual authority above temporal rule.

Guénon argues that healthy societies keep that order, with kings guarding a law they do not invent and priests guarding the truth that law serves. When rulers claim the highest place for themselves, he says, decline and confusion follow in every part of life. The book is central to his work. Readers meeting Guénon for the first time often start here, because his whole system appears in it in compact form.
lessons-of-the-war-being-comments-from-w:
Spenser Wilkinson published his weekly war comments as Lessons of the War in 1900. Archibald Constable issued the book in London and Philadelphia. Chapters begin with the eve of the South African war.

Titles trace a week's campaign, playing with fire, and Buller's problem. Wilkinson asks how weak policy leads to bad strategy. He presses for reinforcements and calls the war the nation's business. His comments ran while the Boer War still unfolded. Readers get a military critic thinking in public, week by week. A chapter asks simply for the right man to lead. Wilkinson later became a noted military historian at Oxford.
nasa-tm-19660001934-a-system-for-automat:
Neal E Reid at Goddard described a system that gathers radiation test data on its own, in this August 1965 report. Semiconductor devices, the parts of modern circuits, change under radiation. Testing them means logging many readings over long exposures. Reid's system uses a digital clock, a scanner, and a relay box to collect those readings automatically.

Automatic logging removes hours of hand recording. It also cuts the errors that creep into hand-copied tables. Radiation data decided which electronic parts could fly. A system that gathered the data steadily, day and night, made those judgments faster and firmer for the engineers who relied on them.
nasa-tm-19660015402-on-the-production-of:
P B Abraham, K A Brunstein, and T L Cline at Goddard asked where low-energy cosmic ray electrons come from, in this February 1966 paper. Cosmic ray electrons arrive from space at many energies. The low-energy ones are the hardest to trace, because the solar wind bends their paths and changes their energies on the way in. Their origins could lie in the Sun, or far beyond it.

Sorting those origins shapes models of how particles fill the solar system. The paper belongs to Goddard's energetic particles preprint series. Such electrons also affect the radiation setting near Earth. A clear account of their production helps both pure science and the practical work of shielding crews and instruments.
nasa-tm-19670019840-description-and-desi:
Loren W. Acker, Nick J. Sekas, and Seymour Lieblein, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, describe a test facility in this memorandum. The facility serves liquid-metal radiators and condensers, hardware that dumps waste heat from space power systems. Liquid metals carry heat well, but they must be tested on the ground first.

The contents show the facility's layout in detail. Separate loops handle heating, vapor, and cooling duties. Component sections cover piping, material selection, stress calculations, and pressure losses. A primary heater gets its own treatment. The document is a design record for engineers building or using such rigs.
nasa-tm-19710018260-the-effects-of-charg:
Walter A. Wappaus conducted this test series on spacecraft mirror coatings that control temperature by reflecting sunlight. The coatings were silvered and aluminized FEP Teflon films used as second surface mirrors. In orbit such coatings face electrons, protons, and ultraviolet light, all of which can darken them and spoil their cooling power.

Wappaus irradiated both coatings with electrons and protons at two energy levels and with ultraviolet light as strong as five suns. He also tested ultraviolet and charged particles together, as real space delivers them. The results show both coatings suffer more from higher-energy protons than from electrons of the same energy. Combined exposure hurt more than particles alone at high doses, while ultraviolet alone in vacuum left the coatings virtually unchanged.
nasa-tm-19710022892-skylab-three-axis-mo:
Michael T. Borelli of the Marshall Space Flight Center and Jack Templeton of Sperry Rand Corporation reported these results in June 1971. Their report was issued as NASA TM X-64609. Their subject was STAMP, the Skylab three-axis motion platform. The platform tilts and turns a load in three axes to mimic spacecraft motion for tests and training.

The report describes the system, states its performance requirements, and then walks through the test program section by section. Tests covered frequency response, transient response, position and rate accuracy, stiffness, and gimbal friction. A parameter sensitivity test and a discussion with recommendations close the main text. Illustrations show control moment gyros mounted in torque measuring fixtures on the load platform, the hardware the platform was built to exercise.
nasa-tm-19720023243-launch-vehicle-syste: Launch vehicle system requirements and restraints for the ERTS-A spacecraft is a NASA technical memorandum on launching an Earth resources satellite. The hosted sample is garbled optical character text, and it preserves no readable title page, author name, or date. Its abstract, kept with the record, says the report lists what the spacecraft required of the Delta launch vehicle. It also covers the shroud, the launch complex, and the range. Agencies involved in the launch could use those limits to coordinate their work.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-53-1-corinth:
First Corinthians, in the version of Douay-Rheims, an English rendering of the Latin Vulgate revised by Bishop Richard Challoner over 1749 to 1752. Its two parts first appeared at Rheims in 1582 and at Douay in 1609 and 1610. An introduction says Paul treats several matters of faith, morals, and church discipline in the letter.

Chapter one rebukes divisions about teachers. The world, Paul argues, was to be saved by preaching of the cross, not by human wisdom or fine speech. Paul writes as a called apostle, with Sosthenes, to a church in Corinth. Quarrels over leaders give the letter its start. From that local split, Paul moves to questions that still shape church teaching.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-54-2-corinth:
Second Corinthians, in Douay-Rheims English drawn from the Latin Vulgate, in the revision Bishop Richard Challoner finished across 1749 to 1752. Rheims in 1582 supplied the New Testament, Douay in 1609 and 1610 the Old Testament. An introduction says Paul recounts his sufferings and the graces God gave him. The letter was written in the same year as the first and sent by Titus from Macedonia.

Chapter one speaks of Paul's troubles in Asia. His failure to come was not levity, he insists, and his doctrine is constant and sincere. Paul writes with Timothy to the church at Corinth and all the saints nearby. Defence of his own ministry, unusual in a letter, fills much of what follows.
the-fourth-r:
George O. Smith wrote The Fourth R as a novel of a boy raised to a fierce pitch of learning, under a copyright of 1959. James Quincy Holden is five years old on the first page.

Jimmy's fifth birthday starts at seven with cocktails for the grown-ups, while he sips ginger ale. His gifts run to Kipling's Jungle Tales, a small planetarium, and a kit for building a Geiger counter with real samples to test. He picks the dinner menu and the music, then wins at bridge. Smith builds a tale of what a brilliant child, pushed by grown schemes, might do to the world that made him.
the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-dicti:
Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, in the version published in 1913 by the C. & G. Merriam Co. of Springfield, Mass., under the direction of Noah Porter, covers English words in alphabetical order. The portion here holds the letter R. It begins with a note on the letter itself, calling it a vocal consonant and a liquid, and tracing its form through Greek and Latin.

Word entries follow, each with pronunciation, origin, and sense. Early entries include Ra, the prefix Ra-, Raash for the electric catfish, Rab, and Rabat. The section also explains the phrase the three Rs for reading, writing, and arithmetic. Notes mark old or local uses and cite writers as support.
tom-swift-and-his-motor-cycle-or-fun-and:
Victor Appleton's first Tom Swift book opens on a country road, where two lads in a touring car urge red-haired Andy to shove the spark lever and make a record. Contents promise twenty-five chapters of fun and adventures on the road, starting with a narrow escape. Tom overhears something, suffers a smash-up, and gets his motor-cycle.

Later headings bring a vindictive tramp, men in an auto, a storm, a strange mansion, pursuit, and unexpected help. Mr. Swift despairs midway, and a man called Eradicate saws wood and gives a clue. Readers get the series launch, with speed and suspicion from the first page.
